intro: Who has argued what, from Griesbach to the present. Markan priority with Q (the Two-Source hypothesis) has been the majority view since the late nineteenth century, and it still is. Its main rivals have been the Griesbach (Two-Gospel) hypothesis, chiefly in North America since 1964, and the Farrer hypothesis, chiefly in Britain since the 1990s. Matthean Posteriority, proposed by Storr in 1786 and Wilke in 1838, has had a small revival since Huggins (1992) and MacEwen (2015). This list samples the leading advocates of every position. It is not a sample of opinion: the minority views are over-represented, and the bars do not show how the field divides. No formal survey of scholars' opinion exists. Each entry names the work where the position is stated. Entries marked unchecked rest on the standard literature rather than on a text cited here.

items.name: Johann Jakob Griesbach
items.note: *Commentatio* (1789–90), announced in 1783: Mark abbreviated and combined Matthew and Luke, switching to Luke wherever he left Matthew's order. Griesbach also produced the first synopsis (1776).

items.name: C. G. Wilke
items.note: *Der Urevangelist*: Mark first, and Matthew took the double tradition from Luke. No sayings source. Modern advocates of Matthean Posteriority claim him as their forerunner.

items.name: C. H. Weisse
items.note: *Die evangelische Geschichte*: Matthew and Luke both used canonical Mark and Papias's λόγια (“oracles”). Carlson calls this the first formulation of the Two-Source hypothesis; Kloppenborg a forerunner of it. In 1856 he went back to an Ur-Markus.

items.name: H. J. Holtzmann
items.note: *Die synoptischen Evangelien*: source A (a proto-Mark) and the sayings source Λ. He dropped the proto-Mark by 1886. Around 1880 he also allowed, with E. Simons, that Luke made some secondary use of Matthew.

items.name: Johannes Weiss
items.note: First used the siglum Q (*Quelle*, “source”) for the sayings source in place of “the λόγια”.

items.name: Paul Wernle
items.note: *Die synoptische Frage*: Matthew and Luke used Mark itself, so no proto-Mark is needed and Q is more or less the double tradition. This became the classic German form.

items.name: B. H. Streeter
items.note: *The Four Gospels*: Mark, Q, M and L (a “four-document hypothesis”), plus Proto-Luke. This became the classic British statement. He explained the minor agreements chiefly as independent editing and textual assimilation.

items.name: B. C. Butler
items.note: *The Originality of St Matthew*: Matthew first, Mark used Matthew, and Luke used both, with no Q. He named the “Lachmann fallacy”: order shows only that Mark is the middle term, not that Mark came first.

items.name: Austin Farrer
items.note: “On Dispensing with Q”: once Luke's use of Matthew is credible, Q loses its reason to exist. Kloppenborg notes that the essay had little immediate effect.

items.name: Robert L. Lindsey
items.note: “A Modified Two-Document Theory” (*NovT* 6): Luke first, then Mark, then Matthew, with shared lost sources. This became the basis of the “Jerusalem school”.

items.name: William R. Farmer
items.note: *The Synoptic Problem*: attacked the logic of the Markan hypothesis and revived Griesbach, later as the “Two-Gospel hypothesis”. Kloppenborg calls it the most important development since Streeter.

items.name: Joseph A. Fitzmyer
items.note: “The Priority of Mark and the ‘Q’ Source in Luke”, and *Luke I–IX* (1981), pp. 73–75: a standard statement of the reasons Luke did not use Matthew.

items.name: M.-É. Boismard
items.note: *Synopse des quatre Évangiles*, vol. 2: several lost documents and intermediate editions of the Gospels. Restated in English in “The Two-Source Theory at an Impasse” (1979).

items.name: W. G. Kümmel
items.note: *Einleitung in das Neue Testament* (17th edn; ET 1975): the standard textbook defence of the Two-Source hypothesis in its generation.

items.name: Frans Neirynck
items.note: *The Minor Agreements of Matthew and Luke against Mark*: a full catalogue. He argued that they come from Matthew and Luke independently editing Mark, together with textual factors, and led the Leuven defence of the hypothesis.

items.name: Michael D. Goulder
items.note: *Midrash and Lection in Matthew* (1974) and *Luke: A New Paradigm* (1989). He went further than Farrer and dispensed with M, L and most oral tradition as well, and he linked the Gospels to a lectionary. Later Farrer scholars dropped both moves.

items.name: H. Benedict Green
items.note: *The Gospel according to Matthew* (1975). Also “The Credibility of Luke's Transformation of Matthew” (1984).

items.name: John Drury
items.note: *Tradition and Design in Luke's Gospel*: Luke used Mark and Matthew freely. Like Goulder, he gave Luke very little independent oral tradition.

items.name: Bernard Orchard
items.note: *Matthew, Luke and Mark* (1976), and *The Order of the Synoptics* with Harold Riley (1987). Co-author of the 1984 Jerusalem statement of the Two-Gospel hypothesis.

items.name: Robert H. Gundry
items.note: *Matthew* commentary, and “Matthean Foreign Bodies” (1992): Luke used Q and Mark, but also knew Matthew, which explains some minor agreements.

items.name: Christopher M. Tuckett
items.note: *The Revival of the Griesbach Hypothesis* (1983) and *Q and the History of Early Christianity* (1996): the leading British defender of Q, against both Griesbach and Farrer.

items.name: Ulrich Luz
items.note: *Das Evangelium nach Matthäus* (EKK; ET *Matthew 1–7*, 1989): the major German Matthew commentary works with Mark and Q, but a Q that circulated in recensions (QMt close to the common form, QLk much enlarged). For the minor agreements, which he calls the one serious difficulty for the Two-Source hypothesis, he allows slightly differing versions of Mark.

items.name: John S. Kloppenborg
items.note: *The Formation of Q*: Q was a written Greek document that grew in stages, a sapiential layer expanded by a deuteronomistic one. Later he co-edited the *Critical Edition of Q* (2000) and wrote *Excavating Q* (2000).

items.name: Robert H. Stein
items.note: *The Synoptic Problem: An Introduction* (2nd edn *Studying the Synoptic Gospels*, 2001): the standard evangelical textbook for Markan priority and Q.

items.name: W. D. Davies & Dale C. Allison
items.note: *Matthew* (ICC), vol. 1: Luke shows no knowledge of Matthew's additions to Mark, and sometimes Matthew and sometimes Luke has the more original wording. Allison returned to the question in 2022, arguing that Luke's Sermon on the Plain is not a rewriting of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount.

items.name: E. P. Sanders & Margaret Davies
items.note: *Studying the Synoptic Gospels*: “Matthew used Mark and Luke used them both”, with what they call a “rather substantial modification”. Both evangelists also had other sources for the sayings. They judged that the Two-Source and Griesbach hypotheses both “break down”.
items.ref: Sanders & Davies 1989, pp. 112, 117, as quoted in Goodacre 2002c; Kloppenborg 2023, p. 16

items.name: John Wenham
items.note: *Redating Matthew, Mark and Luke*: Matthew first, and early dates for all three.

items.name: Ronald V. Huggins
items.note: “Matthean Posteriority: A Preliminary Proposal” (*NovT* 34): Mark, then Luke, then Matthew. This began the modern revival of Wilke's view.

items.name: David R. Catchpole
items.note: *The Quest for Q*: detailed studies arguing that Q had its own distinctive themes and structure.

items.name: Eric Franklin
items.note: *Luke: Interpreter of Paul, Critic of Matthew*: Luke wrote knowing Matthew and in part correcting it.

items.name: Harry T. Fleddermann
items.note: *Mark and Q* (1995) and *Q: A Reconstruction and Commentary* (2005): Q existed, and Mark knew and used it.

items.name: A. J. McNicol, D. L. Dungan & D. B. Peabody
items.note: *Beyond the Q Impasse: Luke's Use of Matthew* (1996), and its sequel *One Gospel from Two* (2002) on Mark's use of Matthew and Luke. These are the Griesbach school's team commentaries.
items.ref: McNicol, Dungan & Peabody 1996; Peabody, Cope & McNicol 2002; Kloppenborg 2023, p. 15

items.name: James M. Robinson
items.note: Co-editor of *The Critical Edition of Q* (with Hoffmann and Kloppenborg), the International Q Project's text. His “LOGOI SOPHON” essay (German 1964; ET 1971) set Q's genre among sayings of the wise.

items.name: Martin Hengel
items.note: *The Four Gospels and the One Gospel of Jesus Christ*: Luke before Matthew, and Matthew used Mark and probably Luke. He still allowed a sayings (logia) source.

items.name: David Alan Black
items.note: *Why Four Gospels?*: Matthew first, then Luke, then Mark. Mark draws on Peter's preaching of Matthew and Luke.

items.name: Mark Goodacre
items.note: *The Case Against Q*: Markan priority affirmed and Q rejected. Unlike Goulder, he lets Luke draw on oral tradition as well as Mark and Matthew, and he has no lectionary theory. *The Fourth Synoptic Gospel* (2025) extends the argument to John.

items.name: James D. G. Dunn
items.note: “Altering the Default Setting” (*NTS* 49) and *Jesus Remembered*: Q for the close double-tradition agreements, and oral performance for the loose ones.

items.name: Paul Foster
items.note: “Is It Possible to Dispense with Q?” (*NovT* 45): a reply to Goodacre and the Farrer case. He also wrote on Matthew's doublets (2016) and Streeter's minor sources (2023).

items.name: Ken Olson
items.note: “Unpicking on the Farrer Theory” (in *Questioning Q*): Luke does not have to unpick Matthew's additions from Mark sentence by sentence. Also argued that Luke's Lord's Prayer is an abridgement of Matthew's (2015).

items.name: Mark A. Matson
items.note: “Luke's Rewriting of the Sermon on the Mount” (in *Questioning Q*): Luke's Sermon on the Plain read as a deliberate reworking of Matthew's sermon.

items.name: Delbert Burkett
items.note: *Rethinking the Gospel Sources* (2004, 2009) and *The Case for Proto-Mark* (2018): none of the Synoptics used another directly. Q was more than one document.

items.name: Robert A. Derrenbacker Jr.
items.note: *Ancient Compositional Practices and the Synoptic Problem*: ancient authors worked from scrolls and memory, not at desks. Measured against that practice, Matthew's and Luke's use of Mark and Q is more plausible than the alternatives.

items.name: James R. Edwards
items.note: *The Hebrew Gospel and the Development of the Synoptic Tradition*: Luke drew on a Hebrew Gospel, and Matthew is later than Luke (pp. 245–252).

items.name: Andris Abakuks
items.note: Statistical papers (2006–2012) and *The Synoptic Problem and Statistics* (2015). Matthew's and Luke's retention of Mark's words is strongly dependent, which fits contact and strains independence. Whether Luke used Matthew or the reverse was inconclusive, though a 2006 model preferred the Farrer order.

items.name: Dennis R. MacDonald
items.note: *Two Shipwrecked Gospels*: an expanded Q (“the Logoi of Jesus”) used by Mark, Matthew and Luke. Luke also used Matthew.

items.name: Francis Watson
items.note: *Gospel Writing*: Luke used Mark and Matthew. He suggests Luke copied some Matthean sayings into a notebook for later use. Tuckett's reply (2018) targets this model and its “L/M”.

items.name: Alexander Damm
items.note: *Ancient Rhetoric and the Synoptic Problem: Clarifying Markan Priority* (BETL 252): tests direction of dependence by the rhetorical virtues of clarity and propriety, and finds for Markan priority. A student of Kloppenborg's, he had earlier argued (SBL 2003) that in the Beelzebul controversy Luke's use of Q is more plausible than Luke's use of Matthew.

items.name: Jason D. BeDuhn
items.note: *The First New Testament*: Marcion did not cut down Luke. He adopted an existing gospel.

items.name: Markus Vinzent
items.note: *Marcion and the Dating of the Synoptic Gospels*: Marcion's Gospel came first, and the canonical Synoptics respond to it.

items.name: Sarah E. Rollens
items.note: *Framing Social Criticism in the Jesus Movement: The Ideological Project in the Sayings Gospel Q* (WUNT 2/374): a social reading of Q's ideology.

items.name: John C. Poirier & Jeffrey Peterson
items.note: Editors of *Marcan Priority without Q* (LNTS 455), the first multi-author volume on the Farrer hypothesis, with a reply from Kloppenborg. Poirier also argued for Luke working from wax tablets (2012, 2023).

items.name: Robert K. MacEwen
items.note: *Matthean Posteriority* (LNTS 501), the first monograph on the view. It was prompted by Huggins's 1992 article. Kloppenborg cites it for problems with Farrer's Luke.

items.name: Giovanni B. Bazzana
items.note: *Kingdom of Bureaucracy* (BETL 274): Q's political theology read as the outlook of Galilean village scribes.

items.name: Alan Kirk
items.note: *Q in Matthew*: Matthew's handling of Q fits ancient scribal and memory practice. Kirk finds Farrer's Luke implausible on those grounds and continued the debate with Eve and Goodacre (2017, 2023).

items.name: Alan Garrow
items.note: “Streeter's ‘Other’ Synoptic Solution” (*NTS* 62): Matthew used Luke, sometimes conflating Luke with one of Luke's small sources. One such source survives in Didache 1.2–5a. He has kept up the debate with Goodacre (2017–2023).

items.name: Craig A. Evans
items.note: Defends the Two-Source hypothesis in *The Synoptic Problem: Four Views*.

items.name: David B. Peabody
items.note: Defends the Two-Gospel hypothesis in *Four Views*. Co-author of the Griesbach team volumes of 1996 and 2002.

items.name: Rainer Riesner
items.note: Presents the “Orality and Memory Hypothesis” in *Four Views*: oral tradition and memory, with some written aids, rather than one Gospel copying another.

items.name: Joseph Verheyden
items.note: Co-editor of *An Early Reader of Mark and Q* (BiTS 21), *New Studies in the Synoptic Problem* (2011) and the Loyola volume (2023). He works within the Two-Source framework.
items.ref: Verheyden & Van Belle 2016; Foster et al. 2011; Andrejevs et al. 2023

items.name: Christoph Heil & Daniel A. Smith
items.note: Co-editors, with Gertraud Harb, of *Built on Rock or Sand? Q Studies: Retrospects, Introspects and Prospects* (2018). Smith has argued that the Gospel used by Marcion lacked several of the minor agreements, which if right would put some of them down to later Matthean influence on the text of Luke.

items.name: Markus Tiwald
items.note: *Kommentar zur Logienquelle* (2019; English 2020) and editor of *The Q Hypothesis Unveiled* (2020).

items.name: Jens Schröter
items.note: “Key Issues Concerning the Q Hypothesis”: keeps Q as a source but doubts that its wording can be reconstructed.

items.name: Olegs Andrejevs
items.note: *Apocalypticism in the Synoptic Sayings Source* (2019) and articles in *NTS* and *JSNT* (2021–22) testing the Farrer and Matthean Posteriority alternatives. Co-editor of the Loyola volume (2023).
items.ref: Andrejevs 2019; Andrejevs 2021; Andrejevs 2022b; Andrejevs et al. 2023

items.name: Eric Eve
items.note: *Relating the Gospels* and *Solving the Synoptic Puzzle*: the fullest case for the Farrer hypothesis since Goodacre. It draws on memory and ancient imitation, and he concedes that some data fit neither hypothesis neatly.

items.name: Matthias Klinghardt
items.note: *The Oldest Gospel* (German 2015): a reconstruction of Marcion's Gospel as the source of all four canonical Gospels, which takes the place of Q.

items.name: Richard Bauckham
items.note: Held Q for most of his career and now uses Matthean Posteriority as a working hypothesis. His objection to Farrer's Luke is “the how, not the why” of Luke's rearrangement. He remains “99%” convinced of Markan priority.

items.name: John S. Kloppenborg
items.note: *Oxford Handbook* survey: at the end of the twentieth century the Two-Source, Farrer and Griesbach hypotheses “remain the best supported”. He calls for “humility” and against announcing that any hypothesis has been “discredited”.

items.name: Paul Foster
items.note: *Oxford Handbook* chapter on M, L and Proto-Luke: these sources now draw “little significant attention”. The double tradition still needs Q or direct dependence to explain it.

items.name: Chakrita M. Saulina
items.note: “Competitive Traditions” (BiTS 44): the Beelzebul controversy read as Matthew developing Luke.

items.name: Jeffrey M. Tripp
items.note: Statistical study of the minor agreements (BiTS 44): where results are clear, Luke influences Matthew. He describes himself as exploring Matthean Posteriority rather than committed to it.

items.name: Sophie Robert Hayek, Jacques Istas & Frédérique Rey
items.note: Machine-learning stylometry: Luke's triple tradition comes from Mark, not Matthew. They judge the Two-Source hypothesis most likely and warn that the dataset is small.

items.name: Simon J. Joseph
items.note: Co-editor of the Loyola volume (BiTS 44, 2023), whose essay “The End of Q Studies: Contemporary Reflections” takes stock of Q research from within it.

items.name: James W. Barker
items.note: *Writing and Rewriting the Gospels*: Mark, then Matthew using Mark, then Luke using both (no Q), and John using all three.

items.name: Christopher M. Tuckett
items.note: “Matthean Posteriority: Did Matthew Use Luke?” (*NovT* 67): Matthew's failure to use material in Luke that would have suited him counts against the view.
